**MISSION::** **Antenna is a 501(c)(3) non-profit multidisciplinary cultural institution presenting exhibitions, public programs, publishing, and regranting located in New Orleans.**
Antenna is made up of a diverse staff & board that operates 2 spaces in New Orleans – Antenna:3718 St. Claude and Antenna:6330 St. Claude (which also hosts Paper Machine\*). We provides financial, curatorial, professional, residential support for BIPOC, LGBTQ-GNC+, women, immigrant, and other abled\*\* cultural contributors and cultural bearers who produce visual and performance art; digitally printed book arts; participatory and socially engaged projects in public space at the intersection of Gender and Identity, the Environment, Equity, Renewable Resources, Abolition, Restorative Justice, and the histories of the Gulf South. 
Antenna produces contemporary programs supporting emerging creative individuals, collectives and collaborations through: Art Exhibitions; Publications and Digital Print Production; Public Programs, Fiscal Sponsorships; the Antenna Collective , Platforms Regranting, and Residencies. If you are interested in learning more about our work, pl ease see our annual report.

# BigTown Gallery is pleased to announce its 2026 season
BigTown Gallery is pleased to announce its 2026 season, opening with _Grand Finale_, an exhibition dedicated to the work of Hugh Townley (1923–2008), the acclaimed sculptor and printmaker whose more than five-decade career combined material rigor with inventive, deeply personal form. A frequent early presence at the gallery, Townley played a formative role in shaping its vision and community, bringing both his extensive experience—as a longtime educator at Brown University and an artist exhibited at institutions including the Museum of Modern Art—and his generous spirit of collaboration to its development. Known for his intricate wood constructions, dynamic reliefs, and later explorations in plywood and color, his work reflects a singular visual language informed by nature, Indigenous traditions, and global spiritual inquiry. The 2026 season will also feature the return of our FILM/TALK/FOOD series with the Wild and Scenic Film Festival’s _Best of the Fest_ selection, as well as the third year of _My Place Photography Workshop 3.0_, a professional development photography workshop led by Jim Dow and Cassandra Klos.
For more than two decades, BigTown Gallery has been rooted in a region shaped by independent artists working within a vital, alternative creative culture. Early on, we were drawn to a generation educated in the years following World War II—many supported by the GI Bill—whose influence helped establish the region’s respected MFA programs. Since then, the gallery has remained committed to presenting the depth and significance of their work, often through exhibitions that trace the arc of an artist’s career for a regional audience.
Now in its third decade, and in partnership with the nonprofit BigTown Projects, the gallery continues to expand its program with exhibitions by contemporary artists addressing the complexities of a changing world. At the same time, a core group of artists remains central to the gallery’s program and ongoing support.
Work is available through the BT—VT website, at exhibitions held in the gallery and at the Stable, and through select art fairs.

# Who We Are
Chicago Artists Coalition (CAC) is a nonprofit organization dedicated to supporting contemporary Chicago artists and curators at pivotal stages of their careers. Founded in 1974 by artists advocating for rights, resources, and visibility, CAC has played a lasting role in shaping Chicago’s cultural landscape while evolving to meet the needs of the city’s creative community. Today, CAC provides residency programs, exhibitions, professional development, and access to critical resources that help artists and curators sustain meaningful practices.

**Creativity Explored is pleased to present *Drawn Together*, a group exhibition celebrating human connection and the expressive power of an artist’s line.**

Featuring works in a variety of media, the exhibition explores gatherings of figures, including friends, families, teams, bandmates, dancers, revelers, and partners in arms. Through visions of their shared joy, love, and camaraderie, these works reflect humanity’s need for connection and belonging.

…

Across the exhibition, communal moments are variously framed by sparsely described, richly patterned, or visually dense environments, ranging from the local supermarket to the athletic field, and from the dance floor to the family dining table. Connection is often established through physical touch, coordinated movement, and a sharing of mutual passions and talents. Gallery Wild showcases contemporary fine art
inspired by wildlife, open spaces, and the spirit
of the American West. Owned and operated
by Jackson Hole wildlife painter, Carrie Wild,
the gallery reflects a deep connection to nature
shaped by years spent observing and studying
the wild. The collection features both established
and emerging artists working in oil, acrylic,
bronze, glass, mixed media, and photography.

Each piece captures the beauty and power of
wild places. Gallery Wild’s mission is to inspire
collectors and foster a deeper appreciation for
conserving wildlife and natural landscapes for
future generations.

*Standing Tall* is a powerful exhibition by internationally acclaimed American painter René Romero Schuler, celebrating the strength, vulnerability, and resilience of the human spirit. Through her signature richly textured, semi-abstract feminine figures, Schuler explores the beauty found in life’s experiences and the quiet strength that emerges from them. With a distinguished career spanning exhibitions across the United States, Europe, and Asia, and works held in permanent museum and institutional collections, Schuler invites viewers to embrace the experiences that shape us and recognize the resilience found in standing tall.

Legacy Gallery is one of the top Scottsdale art galleries for Western art. Located in Old Town, our gallery offers collectors and enthusiasts an exceptional selection of fine art from both established and emerging local artists. As one of the leading old town Scottsdale art galleries, we provide a curated experience that highlights the very best works available.
Experience art like never before during the Scottsdale Artwalk and our gallery openings. Legacy Gallery, a leading art gallery in Scottsdale, invites you to explore new exhibitions, [meet the artists](https://legacygallery.com/artists/), and engage with the local art community. Whether you’re a seasoned collector or simply enjoy discovering unique pieces, our events make connecting with art and culture in Scottsdale, inspiring, memorable, and fun!
At Legacy Gallery, we celebrate the contemporary art Scottsdale loves and the rich traditions that only Western art can achieve. Our collection includes vibrant art of all styles and works by many prominent and talented artists. This offers visitors a diverse selection of pieces that capture the spirit and beauty of the region. From modern interpretations to classic Western landscapes, and fine jewelry, our gallery showcases art that resonates with collectors, investors, and art lovers alike!

Mary Martin Gallery of Fine Art was founded in 2004 by Mary Martin and quickly became a beloved destination for art collectors and enthusiasts visiting Charleston from around the world. Mary believed deeply in celebrating art in all its forms, with a special passion for painters and sculptors whose work combined originality, beauty, and emotional depth. Through her vision and dedication, the gallery built a loyal community of collectors and artists over two decades.

Today, the gallery enters a new chapter as artists Silvia and Dru Blair reopen the space with the intention of honoring Mary’s legacy while giving the gallery new life. Alongside continuing to showcase exceptional artists, the gallery will also become a place of artistic learning and inspiration through art classes and creative experiences in the heart of historic Charleston.

Mountain Trails Gallery welcomes visitors to
its elegant 6,500-square-foot space on the
northeast corner of Jackson’s Town Square. Long
recognized as one of the West’s premier fine art
galleries, it represents an exceptional roster of
acclaimed contemporary and Western artists. The
gallery presents a refined collection of paintings
and sculpture, spanning Western, figurative,
wildlife, still life, and landscape subjects. With
a warm and knowledgeable approach, the
Mountain Trails team is pleased to assist both
seasoned and first-time collectors in discovering
and building meaningful art collections.

Medicine Bird Gallery, located next to Jackson
Trading Company, just off the Town Square,
exclusively showcases the photography of
renowned regional photographer, Gary Creandall.

Capturing the essence of the North American
Rockies and its diverse wildlife has been Gary’s
mission for almost 30 years, providing a focus
on the iconic bison and the Grand Teton and
Yellowstone National Parks. While Gary has shared
his world in Jackson Hole since the early 90s, you
can now enjoy the breadth of his photographic
endeavor in a dedicated gallery setting.

# **Romantic Realism Painting & Sculpture Gallery**
[Linda Cordair Headshot Aug 2026](mailto:cordairart@gmail.com?subject=Ask%20Linda%20Cordair)
[Romantic Realism](https://cordair.com/romantic-realism), the movement which renews the high esthetic standards and techniques of pre-20th century ateliers, brings a rebirth of comprehensibility, beauty, romanticism and stylization to contemporary subject matter. The gallery's collection emphasizes themes which celebrate the moments of happiness, joy and success possible to Man on earth. Subject matter includes figurative, narrative, allegorical, still lifes, seascapes and landscapes. Award-winning painters and sculptors of international renown are represented, as well as emerging artists of unique vision and accomplishment. Commissions are available for portraiture, murals, garden and architectural projects.
The Cordairs live in Jackson, WY, with their Labradoodle, Sophie. Quent is a full-time author and painter. Linda manages the gallery and the 30 talented artists they represent.

OPENING: SATURDAY, DECEMBER 5, 2026, 6-9 PM 
Exhibition Runs December 6 - January 17, 2027
Undivine Time by Tia-Simone Gardner revisits 2026, compressing 365 days of lived experience, memory, and reflection into a single timeline: the exhibition's run. The project invites us to examine what has been forgotten, what was actively or necessarily forgotten, and what we are bound to remember. By interrogating both the softness and hardness time reveals, the work seeks to reorient our understanding of temporality across multiple dimensions—weaving together human and more-than-human time, future and past horizons, and dark, uncataloged spaces. Central to this exploration is Undivine Time, a conceptual title directly inspired by Junauda Petrus's evocative writing.

_[**Marietta Patricia Leis and Sharon Brush: With Out, With In**](https://www.turnercarrollgallery.com/brush-leis-exhibition-2026/)_
November 6–December 15, 2026
**[View works in the exhibition](https://www.turnercarrollgallery.com/product-tag/marietta-patricia-leis-sharon-brush-with-out-with-in/)**
Opening celebration: Friday November 6, 4-6pm
Sharon Brush and Marietta Patricia Leis are two artists whose quiet, powerful, and organic work complement each other perfectly. Sharon Brush approaches the construction of each of her vessels as a sculpture—working to create rhythm, flow, reverberation and quiet within each one. Intrigued by contrasts, she moves from slow, sweeping curves to staccato points and ridges; from enclosed space to open passage; from deeply textured surface to river-rock smoothness. Leis’ reductive, expressive visual practice is shaped out of experiments in material process and takes inspiration from the forms of nature, sense of place and the internal landscape. She uses minimal yet deep color palettes across a variety of mediums the viewer can lose themselves in.
_[**Jeanette Pasin Sloan**](https://www.turnercarrollgallery.com/jeanette-pasin-sloan-exhibition-2026/)_
September 25–November 1, 2026
**[View works in the exhibition](https://www.turnercarrollgallery.com/product-tag/jeanette-pasin-sloan-transfiguration/)**
This exhibition will feature the still life paintings of Jeanette Pasin Sloan, whose stunning realist paintings are featured in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Smithsonian Museum, National Gallery, and more. Jeanette Pasin Sloan taught herself to paint as a young mother, putting her children to bed early so she could paint at the kitchen table studio. She obsessively painted the reflective surfaces of her chrome toaster and silver teacups, these everyday objects which we all share and know intimately. Pasin Sloan later earned an MFA from the University of Chicago in art history, where she developed her passion for extending the techniques of old master painters. After mastering oil and watercolor, the artist created a series of fantastic lithographs with Landfall Press.

Dayenu: It Would Have Been Enough, is a solo exhibition by Pittsburgh fiber-artist Louise Silk. Following up from her landmark retrospective at the Heinz History Center in 2024, Dayenu is a career capstone exhibition featuring an all-new body of work being shown together for the first time. The exhibition features hand-sewn works, including art quilts, scrap quilts, flags, kaftans, portraits, and pillows, all made from repurposed fabrics. By working with both her own scraps and found textiles, Silk “brings together separate events and recollections that all contribute to a meaningful visual expression of my life.”

November 14, 2026
As we ease into the season of giving, we're reflecting on the ways the arts enrich our everyday lives. Some are easy to identify, like a beautifully curated gallery wall or a piece of pottery fresh out of the kiln. Others are less tangible, like the friendships formed in a classroom, the confidence gained from trying something new, or the chance to rediscover your inner child while playing in the studio. Here are five reasons we're especially thankful for the arts this season. 1. The spaces that bring people together Galleries, studios, classrooms, and community art centers offer places to gather, meet people, exchange ideas, and find a sense of belonging. At AVA, we're grateful to provide a space where people of all ages and backgrounds can come together, express themselves, and connect through creativity. 2. The artists who share their creativity with the world From established artists to someone picking up a paintbrush for the first time, we're grateful for the people who bring beauty, curiosity, and fresh perspectives into the world. Art takes countless forms, and we're thankful for those who make room in their lives to create, experiment, and share a little piece of themselves with others. 3. The opportunity to keep learning One of the wonderful things about art is that there's no finish line. No matter your age or experience, there's always a new material to explore, a technique to try, or something unexpected to discover. Art reminds us that we can be beginners at any stage of life, and that learning doesn't always have to be about getting something right. Sometimes, the best part is simply seeing where your curiosity takes you. 4. The way art helps us see things differently Art can challenge our assumptions, spark conversations, preserve stories, and introduce us to experiences outside our own. Sometimes, it gives us a moment to stop and appreciate something we might otherwise overlook. We're grateful for the ways art encourages us to stay curious, consider different perspectives, and see the world through someone else's eyes. 5. The people who support the arts A thriving arts community is made possible by the volunteers, instructors, donors, collectors, families, and visitors who show up and make it all possible. You don't have to be an artist to play an important role in the arts. Whether you're attending an exhibition, taking a class, volunteering your time, purchasing a piece of artwork, or introducing someone to their first creative experience, your participation matters. We're grateful for everyone who helps keep the arts alive and accessible in our community. ## Quiet Migrations
Quiet Migrations follows the journey of searching for truth, not unlike the allegory of Plato’s Cave. Migrations also refers to movement in the natural world, where humans and animals move unbound by the illusions of borders. The work reflects on identity, in the perception of self and how our surroundings experience us. 
By layering old maps and migratory diagrams, Escobar’s work connects the seasonal routes of species like monarch butterflies with the quiet, often overlooked journeys of human migration. 
​
Monica uses drawing, assemblage and music to create a deeply personal installation that illuminates a reality she did not fully see until her recent ADHD diagnosis and treatments.

## Sylvia Schieber, “Alaska AIR” Artist Residency and Exhibit, November 2026
Maske Maiden (Sylvia Schieber) is Artist in Residence at Bunnell Arts from November 3- 29, 2026. Her accompanying exhibit opens on Friday, November 6 from 5-7pm with an artist talk at 6pm, alongside artist Rae Diamond. While in residence, she will offer workshops on meditative embroidery and mask-making.
Artist Statement – Maske Maiden (Sylvia Schieber) interweaves mask-making, fiber techniques, and storytelling to create immersive, character-driven worlds that blur ritual, adornment, and identity. “Using fiber techniques and found materials, I create sculptural masks as vessels for memory and possibility. Influenced by my upbringing in an immigrant household shaped by reuse and resourcefulness, I often work with discarded and repurposed materials, drawing attention to their overlooked possibilities. Through world-building, I explore the tension between imagined lives and the forces that shape them.”

_**Curated by Jess Bass & Yue Xu 
October 16 - November 26, 2026

**The exhibition premieres new work by:** Jess Bass, Camille Casemier, Maurício Chades, Corey Smith, Odette Stout, and Yue Xu, who use the metaphor of the rabbit — its body, social structures, habitat, and ecosystem — to playfully explore the dynamics of power within global, complex networks of ecology, economics, government, and politics. _**Molly Blumberg 
October 16 - November 26, 2026
**Opening Reception:** October 16th, 2026, 6:00 PM – 9:00 PM
In Second Hand, Molly Blumberg presents a body of work that embraces processes of un-functioning and re-functioning. Objects slump, reach, and join one another, sometimes seamlessly and sometimes by force. She collects and transforms detritus, exploring what might grow when things are broken apart and reassembled.  A broken chair droops into a bodily blob, bedsprings reach out with new appendages, organic matter is sealed in resin as it decays inside its shell. This work seeks potential in malfunctions and misfires. Out of the breakdown of an intended function objects become something else(…)

##### Gail Wagner and Guests     _Spinoffs_
**_Spinoffs_** is an exhibition of art influenced by textiles. From French tapestries to Japanese Ikat, Blackwork embroidery to Italian damask, Chinese grass-cloth to Ukrainian folk fabric, fiber from around the world serves as muse, sometimes with a shout and sometimes with a whisper. Paintings, digital art, and pyrography reference our collective consciousness of textile history in visual form. An appreciation of fiber and its offshoots unite the works in this eclectic showcase of styles.
##### Jennifer Pettu_s     S{t}imulation_
The work in **_S{t}imulation_** continues my exploration of labor, function, and materiality in an increasingly disconnected and overwhelming world. The rapid proliferation of AI shortcuts, where there is no manual skill required, is disheartening – and means putting hands to material is even more vital to my process. Whether it is a pen, a paintbrush, or a needle and thread, I am marking my journey, with all its human imperfections. I embellish non-traditional materials with riotous texture and color to challenge institutionalized art practices, but also to invite reflection on the ways we are literally losing touch with our environments.

Sarah Barnett: Spectacle of Being
Sarah Barnett: Spectacle of Being
Drawing from medical imagery and emerging technologies, these paintings present the operating theater as a site where the vulnerable human body, apparatus, machine, image and observer converge. They reflect on the strange reality unfolding as once-imagined technologies become increasingly intimate with our lives.

Matthew Behrend: Radiant Echoes
Matthew Behrend: Radiant Echoes
Light settles into metal the way a dream lingers after waking. These patina works mark the signs of arriving somewhere inward: ease, recognition, elements falling into place. Some sounds are heard only after they pass. Come and listen for what returns.

Marcus Lelle: Reclaimed : Renewed
Marcus Lelle: Reclaimed : Renewed
Reclaimed : Renewed explores the relationship between art and artist. By using recycled materials the art becomes sustainable, and incorporating images into wearable pieces, the artist aims to share the tactile experience of creating. This exhibition is comprised of a variety of techniques that show the range of the Cyanotype process.

Leah Rachel Hawker, _Seeking the Sacrosanct_, archival photographic print, 24 x 36 inches, edition of 4, 2026
I am a South African multi-disciplinary artist working across ceramics, embroidery, beadwork, collage and photography. Deeply tied to cultural heritage and storytelling I use traditional woman’s handcrafts in much of my practice. My work is informed by women’s knowledge – past and present. I play with contemporary dialogues of societies notions of self-identity and beauty moulded through mass media, and at the same, time try to make sense of ancient lost wisdoms.
I explore re-matriation and systemic violence and I try to envisage new relationships with the feminine and earth through ancestral knowledge and mythology which could have the potential for healing.

I make mixed media work about: paradox, borders, identity, lineage, peace, and tension. My distinctive drawing style is anchored in an illustration background alongside my mixed heritage (as a Jersey girl with Punjabi and eastern European roots) and a continued, blooming journey of self-discovery.
The Murrah buffalo (“madge”) is part of my family’s folklore. For me, the animal represents a storied gentleness, nourishment, and stability. Though I’ve never seen or met her (the madge) - only heard about her.
## Christine Crook & Pete Fields
So here we are again. This is a house, and these are its clothes. If you are reading this, maybe you‘re paying attention and you’ve noticed the second installment of our adornment to this building we call The Front, an art gallery, an artist collective, a home. This time around, we got louder, more riotous, and decided to offer a full-throttle celebration of this special house, a house that welcomes everyone and offers a place to show and see the art we create in New Orleans.
Or maybe you didn’t notice this building enough before. Maybe the paint color isn’t bright enough, or maybe you just didn’t see a sign letting you know that this is The Front. The old sign had faded and peeled, and the new sign got painted over, and we wanted to make sure you saw this building again. So we dressed it up. And when I say dressed, I mean Fully Dressed, like a New Orleans po-boy, with everything on it, slathered in Duke’s, piled high with lettuce, pickles, and tomatoes. Because the secret ingredient is always more.
This work celebrates The Front, celebrates local art, and celebrates community. It was created by me, Christine Crook, and my husband, Pete Fields. This house has nurtured our creativity and our friendships. It has been a place where we have made things, seen things, met people, laughed, gathered, and become part of something bigger. The Front is a part of our story, and we want to give something back to this house that gave to us.
